W boson. The W boson is a massive elementary particle that mediates the weak nuclear force, responsible for radioactive decay and certain particle interactions. It comes in two charged varieties, W positive and W negative, and was experimentally confirmed in nineteen eighty-three. Its discovery vindicated the electroweak unification theory and remains central to understanding matter's subatomic transformations.

The W boson exists in two charge states: W positive and W negative. This allows it to mediate different decay processes and charge transformations among quarks and leptons. It is extraordinarily massive for a boson—approximately eighty-point-four giga-electron-volts per speed-of-light-squared, nearly eighty times the proton mass. This tremendous mass gives the weak force its characteristically short range of only about one times ten to the negative eighteen meters.

In nineteen eighty-three, Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer experimentally discovered the W boson at CERN using the Super Proton Synchrotron. The discovery earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics. The W boson is responsible for beta decay, where a neutron transforms into a proton by emitting a W negative boson, which then decays into an electron and an antineutrino. This process is crucial to stellar nucleosynthesis. It mediates interactions between leptons like electrons and quarks, enabling fundamental processes in stars where it drives fusion reactions and in the early universe.

The W boson forms part of the electroweak unification, where the W and Z bosons unify electromagnetic and weak interactions at energies above approximately one hundred giga-electron-volts. This prediction was confirmed at the Large Hadron Collider. The W boson cannot be produced or observed directly. It is detected only through its decay products—leptons and quarks—in particle accelerator experiments, revealing itself through missing energy signatures.

The theory behind the W boson was developed decades before its experimental confirmation. Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam, and Steven Weinberg predicted it theoretically in the nineteen sixties as part of the electroweak theory, years before experimental confirmation in the nineteen eighties. Today, production of W bosons occurs only at the most powerful particle accelerators. The Large Hadron Collider produces millions of W bosons annually, each decaying in picoseconds to reveal its identity through detector signatures.
